Five days later Belgium would restore the kid. This Sunday belongs to Leclerc.
A home-soil weekend for Russell, a first 2026 win for Leclerc, a dent in Antonelli's march.

Antonelli wins Monza from 19th. First Italian home win since 1966.
Grid 19, chequered flag 1. Pierre Gasly's first pole. A Mercedes one-two. A 66-point lead. History in the grandstands.
6 September. Antonelli 1:51:15.281 from P19. Russell +3.857, Verstappen +14.718. First Italian Monza winner since Ludovico Scarfiotti.

Why this one matters: home races are supposed to go wrong. This one went from nineteenth to first, and Italy had not done that at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966. No one had won from as far back as 19th since John Watson from 22nd at Long Beach in 1983.

Pierre Gasly took Alpine's first pole. Russell led by lap two. Antonelli climbed through a race that lasted 1:51:15.281 and passed his teammate late. Russell second by 3.857. Verstappen third by 14.718. Norris fourth, Piastri fifth, Hamilton sixth. Leclerc, Alonso and Stroll did not finish. Fastest lap Antonelli, 1:23.504. BBC, Wikipedia and ESPN agree on the classified order.

Championship: Antonelli 267, Russell 201, Hamilton 191, Norris 171, Leclerc 155. Constructors: Mercedes 468, Ferrari 346, McLaren 287. Seventh win of the season. Next is Madrid, a new circuit, 11-13 September.
A home win, a 66-point lead, a constructors grip, a new track next week.

Semis done. Bronze on Saturday. The final on Sunday. How the last chapter of World Cup 2026 is shaping up.

## The Quiet Between Storms

There are no fixtures on 16 July. After a semi-final week that sent Spain and Argentina to the final and France and England into the bronze match, the tournament finally exhales.

That pause matters. Final-week football is not only tactics and travel. It is recovery rooms, quiet hotel corridors, and the strange mix of relief and dread that comes when only one match remains between you and history.

## How We Got Here

Spain beat France 2-0 in Dallas on 14 July, a semi-final of control and late quality. Argentina beat England 2-1 in Miami on 15 July, surviving a late surge to book a return to the biggest night.

Those results set a clean bracket for the first 48-team World Cup:
- **18 July, Miami**: France vs England (third place)

The Greatest World Cup Upsets of All Time
When the underdogs bit back and the world stopped breathing
From Ecuador toppling Germany in 2026 to Saudi Arabia's 2022 miracle - when football's giants fall, everything changes.

## The Beautiful Lie We Tell Ourselves

We say we love a giant-killing. We say it every tournament, every group stage draw, every time a minnow gets paired with a behemoth and pundits solemnly explain the gap in quality. We say we love it  -  and then, the moment it actually happens, we genuinely cannot believe our own eyes.

That's the thing about a World Cup upset. It doesn't just surprise you. It rewires your understanding of what football is supposed to be. The script gets torn up in real time, and eighty thousand people in a stadium  -  plus however many millions watching at home  -  all have the same thought at once: *wait, can they actually do this?*

They can. They have. And in 2026, they already have again.

## Pak Doo-ik and the Day England's Empire Crumbled

Let's start in 1966, at Ayresome Park in Middlesbrough, because that's where football's sense of its own order first got a proper shaking. North Korea  -  a nation most of the world couldn't have found on a map  -  arrived at their first and only World Cup having drawn 1-1 with Chile and somehow beaten Italy 1-0 through a single, historic Pak Doo-ik strike on July 19th.

Italy. *Italy.* A nation that had won the World Cup twice. Sent home by a dentist from Pyongyang, if the romanticised version of Pak's profession is to be believed. The Italians returned home to be pelted with rotten tomatoes at Genoa airport. North Korea went to the quarter-finals, went 3-0 up against Portugal before Eusébio reminded everyone that fairy tales have editors, and then quietly disappeared back behind the iron curtain. But the ghost of that result never quite left.

## Senegal's Morning After the Night Before

Fast-forward to June 1st, 2002, in Seoul, and a different kind of history. France arrived in South Korea and Japan as world champions, European champions, the most complete squad on the planet  -  Zidane, Henry, Vieira, Desailly, the full constellation. Senegal, playing their first-ever World Cup match, simply did not care about any of that.

Papa Bouba Diop scored the only goal, wheeled away in joy, and the entire Senegalese bench poured onto the pitch in a moment of such raw, unfiltered happiness that it became one of football's most replayed images. France, astonishingly, went out in the group stage without scoring a single goal. Senegal reached the quarter-finals. The world tilted slightly on its axis and nobody quite corrected it.

## Lusail, November 22nd, 2022

And then there's the one that genuinely felt like it broke physics. Argentina versus Saudi Arabia. Lionel Messi, twelve minutes in, penalty, 1-0. The match everyone expected was happening exactly as expected. Except it wasn't.

Saudi Arabia's offside trap, drilled to a razor's edge by Hervé Renard, had already disallowed three Argentine goals in the first half. The stadium was nervous but Argentina were in control. And then, eleven minutes into the second half, Saleh Al-Shehri equalised, and ninety seconds later Salem Al-Dawsari curled in one of the great World Cup goals  -  a shot of such audacity and precision that even the Argentine players seemed to stop and admire it for a split second.

Final score: Saudi Arabia 2-1 Argentina. The country declared a national holiday the next day. Saudi players sobbed on the pitch. Messi stood and stared. The greatest footballer who ever lived had just been beaten by a team ranked 51st in the world, and the only appropriate response was silence.

## Ecuador 2-1 Germany, Miami, June 2026

And then there is the one still fresh in every football fan's memory. Germany arrived in Miami for their Group E finale having obliterated Ivory Coast 7-1. They needed only a draw. Ecuador, led by a team playing with the hunger of a generation that has spent years knocking on the door of elite football, had other ideas.

Two goals. Two moments of South American brilliance that silenced the German machine completely. The final whistle confirmed the unthinkable: Ecuador topped Group E. Germany, the tournament's form team by goal difference, shuffled out as runners-up in a group they were supposed to win going away.

## Senegal 5-0 Norway, Vancouver, June 2026

If Ecuador's win was a shock, Senegal's annihilation of Norway was something else entirely. Erling Haaland was on the pitch. The whole world watched him absorb five Senegalese goals with the bewildered expression of a man who has arrived at the wrong address.

Ismaila Sarr was unplayable. The Senegalese press was relentless, their combinations crisp, their hunger unmistakable. Norway - a team built around the world's best striker - were simply overwhelmed. Five-nil. The kind of scoreline that makes you re-read it twice.

## Why We Need Them

These upsets matter not because they humiliate the powerful  -  though there's an honest, guilty pleasure in that  -  but because they remind us what sport is actually *for*. Football, at its purest, is proof that preparation and belief and a single moment of genius can overcome almost anything. Rankings, budgets, history, expectation: all of it evaporates the second the ball hits the net.

The giants will fall again. They always do. And we will all pretend we saw it coming.

Three Nations, One Party: The Hosts' Story
From the Rose Bowl to the Azteca to BMO Field, three footballing souls found out who they really are.
For the first time, three countries host the World Cup together. The USA reached the R16, Mexico the R32, and Canada the R32.

There is a moment, sometime around the opening ceremony of any World Cup, when a host nation stops being a country and becomes something closer to a feeling. The flags go up, the streets fill, strangers hug each other in languages they do not share, and the whole place hums with pride that normal life cannot manufacture. Now imagine that happening in three countries at once, across a landmass so vast it contains every climate on earth. That is what the summer of 2026 felt like.

## The Weight of the Sombrero

For Mexico, this was personal in a way that goes beyond football. The Azteca has seen two World Cup finals, in 1970 and 1986. It heard the roar when Maradona dribbled through England. It hosted the Pele generation's coronation.

Mexico won Group A with nine points from three games. Santiago Gimenez was brilliant. The Azteca was a wall of sound. But the knockout rounds brought a familiar heartbreak: Mexico fell to England 3-2 in the Round of 16. El Tri gave everything, pushed one of the tournament's best sides to the limit, and exited with their heads high. The curse of the fifth game remains unbroken, but this generation proved they belong on the biggest stage.

## The Country That Finally Believes

Canada's story is the most moving of the three. This is a country that qualified for its first World Cup in 36 years in 2022 and lost all three group games. Alphonso Davies cried. The whole country cried with him.

In 2026, something shifted. Canada navigated a tough group, held their own against Switzerland and Bosnia, and reached the knockout rounds for the first time in their history. The Round of 32 brought a 1-0 loss to Morocco, but that scoreline does not capture what it meant. Jonathan David tore defences apart at BMO Field. The country now understands what it feels like to care about this sport. The origin story is being written in real time.

## The Giant That Had Everything to Prove

The United States were extraordinary in the group stage. Nine points from three matches. Eight goals scored. Pulisic brilliant, Reyna creative. The MetLife Stadium crowd when the USA beat Paraguay 4-1 on opening night made a sound that belonged in the Maracana.

The knockout rounds brought Belgium, and a 4-1 defeat that exposed the gap between promise and experience. But America answered the question definitively: it cares. Not performatively, not commercially, but in the chest.

## One Party, Three Hearts, Three Stories

What made 2026 unlike anything before it is that the host-nation narrative was braided three times over. Mexico reached the knockout rounds with nine points and a nation dreaming. Canada won their first ever knockout game and a country permanently converted. The United States went as genuine contenders for the first time in their history.

In the end, all three hosts fell before the quarter-finals. But the party they threw across an entire continent will not be forgotten. And the football they played will be the foundation for everything that comes next.

## Why this series matters

Fifty-three years is long enough that people in the building had never seen the last one. The New York Knicks beat the San Antonio Spurs 4-1 in June. Jalen Brunson was Finals MVP. The wait ended.

## What actually happened

Game 1, 3 June: Knicks 105-95 in San Antonio. Game 2, 5 June: Knicks 105-104. Game 3, 8 June: Spurs 115-111 at MSG. Game 4, 10 June: Knicks 107-106, largest Finals comeback on record, 29 points in the second half, OG Anunoby tip-in with 1.2 seconds left. Game 5, 13 June: Knicks 94-90 in San Antonio, Brunson 45, tying Michael Jordan for most points on the road in a series-clinching Finals game.

Mike Brown's Knicks had swept Cleveland in the East. Mitch Johnson's Spurs had beaten Oklahoma City 4-3 in the West. First Finals since 1995 to open with two straight road wins. First since 1993 in which the road team won the first three.

## What it changes

September basketball is not the NBA. Training camp is still ahead. The title is in New York. That is the only basketball sentence the men's league gets on this desk until October.

The Rise of Lamine Yamal and Spain's New Age
How a teenage sensation and a direct style are reinventing La Roja's historical identity.
How a teenage sensation and a direct style are reinventing La Roja's historical identity on the world stage.

## The Boy Who Bypassed the Academy

Lamine Yamal is not playing by the historical rules of Spanish development. While the previous generation of midfielders was drilled to value possession above all else, Yamal plays with the direct, street-football instinct of someone who grew up playing on concrete courts in Rocafonda. He doesn't want to pass sideways; he wants to look the defender in the eye and run at them.

At just 18, he carries the weight of a nation on his slender shoulders, but you wouldn't know it from the way he plays. There is a playground joy in his movements, a casual insolence that makes even the most experienced defenders look clumsy. Spain navigated Group H with 7 points, advancing comfortably - though a surprising 0-0 draw with Saudi Arabia on Matchday 1 served as a reminder that even the most talented squads need their creative spark to ignite.

## Reinventing Tiki-Taka

Spain's historic tiki-taka was beautiful but could occasionally devolve into sterile dominance - thousands of passes with no penetration. This new-look Spain under Luis de la Fuente has kept the technical precision but added rocket fuel to the wings. With Yamal on one flank and Nico Williams on the other, La Roja are suddenly direct, vertical, and terrifying.

Norway's Golden Duo: Haaland and Odegaard's World Cup Dream
After 28 years in the wilderness, Norway returned powered by two of the world's finest talents.

## The Long Wait

For nearly three decades, Norwegian football fans watched the World Cup from the sidelines. Year after year, qualification campaigns ended in near-misses and heartbreak. Then came Erling Haaland and Martin Odegaard, two singular talents who transformed Norway from a nostalgic underdog into one of the most intriguing sides in the tournament.

## The Artist and the Viking

To watch Norway was to watch a study in contrast. Odegaard floated between the lines, constantly scanning the pitch, measuring passes to the millimeter, dictating the tempo. He was the quiet conductor.

Then there was Haaland. He did not float. He stormed. A vertical threat who occupied two defenders at all times, stretching the pitch and creating the space that Odegaard thrives in. When they clicked, it was footballing poetry.

## How It Ended

Norway reached the quarter-finals, their best World Cup performance in history. They swept through a difficult group, conquered the Round of 32 with a 2-1 win over Brazil, then fell to England in a heartbreaking 2-1 quarter-final that went to extra time.

Haaland finished as one of the tournament's top scorers with seven goals. Odegaard controlled games against some of the best midfields in the world. The golden duo delivered everything their nation dreamed of and more. Norwegian football has arrived, and this is only the beginning.

Noskova wastes five championship points. Then she wins Wimbledon.
6-2, 5-7, 6-3. All-Czech. Age 21. Youngest women's champion here since Kvitova in 2011.
Linda Noskova beat Karolina Muchova in an extraordinary Wimbledon final on 11 July. First Slam. Sixth championship point.

## Why this final matters

Wimbledon finals are supposed to be appointments with names you already know. On 11 July the names were Czech, seeded 9 and 10, and friends. Linda Noskova is 21. She is now a Grand Slam champion. That sentence did not exist in June.

## What actually happened

She led 6-2, 5-2. Karolina Muchova won five games in a row and saved five championship points. The second set went 7-5 to Muchova. In the third, Noskova served for it again, hit an ace to set up a sixth championship point, and converted with a service winner. Score: 6-2, 5-7, 6-3.

BBC, The Athletic and CBS logged the same numbers. Youngest women's Wimbledon champion since Petra Kvitova in 2011. First Slam. She had already won Berlin on the grass. Sportico put the prize money around $4.8 million, nearly doubling her career on-court earnings.

## What it changes

On 8 September she met Aryna Sabalenka in the US Open quarter-finals and lost 7-6 (7-1), 3-6, 7-6 (10-7). Wimbledon was the first plot twist. New York ended in a tie-break.

Ryan Fox birdies the 18th and the Claret Jug changes hands
72-68-62-68 = 270. One shot ahead of Cameron Young. Third New Zealander to win a men's major.
The 154th Open at Royal Birkdale, 16-19 July. Fox, 39, birdied the hardest hole of the week to win by one.

## Why this major matters

Majors are supposed to belong to the names on the world ranking. On 19 July a 39-year-old from New Zealand birdied the 18th at Royal Birkdale and became Champion Golfer of the Year. Ryan Fox is the third Kiwi to win a men's major. That is not a cute fact. That is the story.

## What actually happened

Rounds: 72-68-62-68 = 270, ten under. Cameron Young 271 after a Sunday 64. Sam Burns 272. Tommy Fleetwood and Scottie Scheffler tied fourth at 273. The Saturday 62 tied the men's major record for lowest round. CBS called the 36-hole comeback the largest by position to win a men's major.

He began Sunday two behind Burns. He birdied 16 to tie Young at nine under. The 18th had played 161 strokes over par for the field. Fox hit the fairway, the approach to about 12 feet, and the putt. Purse $17.75 million, winner $3.2 million.

## What it changes

The last men's major of 2026 has a new name on it. Scheffler still had the FedEx Cup to play for in August. Fox had the jug. Both sentences are true.

Spain Are World Champions: How the 2026 Final Week Ended
Bronze for England, silver for Argentina, gold for Spain. The first 48-team World Cup has its ending.
Ferran Torres in the 106th minute. Spain 1-0 Argentina after extra time at MetLife. England 6-4 France for bronze, Bukayo Saka with a hat-trick.
CBS News: Spain wins 2026 FIFA World Cup

## Why this week still sits in the chest

A World Cup is a month of noise that collapses into two nights. On 18 July, England and France played a bronze match that FIFA later called barely believable. On 19 July, Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium. If you only remember one sentence, make it this: Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute, from a Nico Williams header, and Spain are champions for the first time since 2010.

## Bronze night in Miami

England 6, France 4, Hard Rock Stadium, 18 July. FIFA's standings piece put names to the chaos. England: Rice 3', Konsa 18', Saka 37', Saka 45+1', Saka 87' from the penalty spot, Bellingham 90+8'. France: Mbappe 48', Barcola 54', Mbappe 66', Dembele 90+6'.

That is a hat-trick for Bukayo Saka in a third-place match. England's best finish since 1966. Ten goals. The highest-scoring bronze final the tournament has on record.

The game was never the final. It still felt like one, because both sides had just lost a semi-final and refused to treat the night as a handshake.

## MetLife, extra time, one punch

Spain vs Argentina on 19 July was the bracket's promise: control against champion steel. Regulation ended 0-0, the first goalless final since 1994. CBS reported Spain outshooting Argentina 20-3. FIFA said 20 attempts to two over 120 minutes. Argentina, reduced to ten after Enzo Fernandez was sent off, failed to register a shot in normal time.

The goal arrived in extra time. Nico Williams headed a cross back into space. Torres, on as a 62nd-minute substitute, smashed it past Emiliano Martinez. Torres later said it was a goal scored by 47 million people, Spain's population, give or take a census.

Attendance 80,663. Referee Slavko Vincic of Slovenia. Torres named man of the match. Martinez made 11 saves, a World Cup final record, and still walked off a runner-up.

Spain conceded one goal in eight matches, a record for a champion. La Roja are unbeaten in their last 38 (29 wins, nine draws) per CBS. They also became the first nation to hold the men's and women's World Cups at once.

A brawl broke out after the whistle. That is in the match record too. Finals do not always end clean.

## What the expanded tournament proved

Forty-eight teams stretched the story across the United States, Mexico and Canada. Group drama still mattered. Knockout nights still hinged on set pieces, rest defence and nerve. The final still felt like the only match in the world.

Spain's path, from FIFA: a shock 0-0 with Cabo Verde to open Group H, then wins over Saudi Arabia, Uruguay, Austria, Portugal, Belgium and France, then Argentina. One goal conceded the whole way.

## The names that travel

- **Spain**: tournament control, one extra-time punch, a second star on the shirt.
- **Argentina**: knockout toughness all the way to the last night, one goal short of back-to-back titles.
- **England**: bronze after a ten-goal classic, Saka the headline.
- **France**: semi-finalists who still carry the most dangerous attacking talent in the sport.

The Last Dance: A Generation Says Goodbye
Time is calling last orders on some of football's greatest careers. Drink it in.
Modrić, Ronaldo and the legends playing their final World Cup. Savour them while you can.

There is a particular kind of grief that arrives before the loss itself. You feel it in the stands when a great player receives the ball and something in your chest tightens  -  not with excitement, but with the sudden, vertiginous awareness that this might be one of the last times. That this is borrowed time, and the debt will come due soon enough.

That is the feeling hovering over North America like a summer heatwave. Football is staging one final curtain call for a generation of players who, quite simply, will never come again.

## The Weight Luka Carries

Luka Modrić is now 40, his presence in this tournament defying logic and biology. He still moves like a man who learned football in a language the rest of the world only half speaks. In the camps for displaced persons in Zadar, as shells fell and his grandfather was murdered by soldiers, a small boy kept a ball close. Decades later, he remains the heartbeat of his nation, his legs somehow still conducting the orchestra when everyone else's have long since given out.

Watch him this time. Watch the way he receives the ball on the half-turn, the way he buys himself a half-second of space through pure intelligence rather than pace he no longer owns. Football is full of players who are fast. It is almost empty of players who think like Modrić. When he is gone, that particular frequency goes silent.

Croatia is a long shot in 2026. That is probably fine. The point is to watch one of the most complete midfielders in the sport's history write his final page, and to understand that you are witnessing it.

## The Argument That Keeps Walking

Cristiano Ronaldo arrived in North America carrying the weight of a legend's final act. He is 41 years old and still here, still competing, still chasing that elusive final dream. 

You can hold complicated opinions about Ronaldo the person and still be staggered by what Ronaldo the athlete has done to the normal laws of sporting mortality. His hunger is either inspiring or exhausting depending on your mood, but it is absolutely, undeniably real.

This is his sixth World Cup. Six. He was 19 in Germany in 2006, a kid with tricks and arrogance and untested promise. Everything that has happened since  -  the Ballon d'Ors, the Champions Leagues, the records that fell like dominoes  -  was built on that raw material. 2026 is the final punctuation mark on a career that has defined an era.

## The Others We Should Name

Do not let the two giants crowd out the rest of the farewell party. Manuel Neuer, still organising the world from his penalty area, the man who redefined what a goalkeeper could be in the modern game. Olivier Giroud, unfashionable and irresistible, scoring goals that the highlight reels somehow always undersell. Thiago Silva, who has been built from reinforced concrete and pure Brazilian belief, marshalling defences at an age when most of his peers are doing punditry.

These are not supporting acts. They are chapters in the same long, beautiful story.

## Why It Matters More Than the Trophy

Here is the uncomfortable truth about great tournaments: the champion, eventually, fades into a footnote for casual fans. What lingers is the imagery  -  Zidane's headbutt, Maradona's Hand of God, Ronaldo weeping on a stretcher in Paris in 2016. Moments attached to people, not to nations.

2026 will give us a champion. It will also give us a goodbye we have not fully prepared ourselves for. The next World Cup will arrive with a new cast. These names, these faces, these particular footballing souls  -  they will be analysts on television, their legs finally at rest.

So watch closely. Savour the Modrić pass that splits a midfield like a needle through silk. Note the Ronaldo chest-puff after a goal, ridiculous and magnificent in equal measure. Let yourself feel the ache of it.

Some goodbyes, you only get once.

Why the 48-Team World Cup Changes Everything
Forget everything you know about the World Cup. The biggest tournament on earth just got bigger and stranger and better.
More teams, more groups, more drama, and a brand-new path to the trophy. Here is what you need to know.

## More Teams, More Stories

There is a moment, every four years, when a country qualifies for the World Cup for the first time and the footage goes everywhere. Players collapsing on the pitch. Fans in streets you have never heard of losing their minds. A coach crying into his hands. That moment is about to happen more often. A lot more often.

FIFA's 48-team World Cup arrives in 2026, spread across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Sixteen more nations get to walk out under those lights. If you think that sounds like mere expansion, you have not been paying attention to what football does to people when it finally shows up at their door.

## The New Shape of the Thing

The old 32-team format had a satisfying geometry: eight groups of four, two go through, clean and simple. The 48-team version reshuffles the deck into twelve groups of four. The top two from each group advance automatically. Then the eight best third-placed finishers squeeze through to a Round of 32.

That means thirty-two sides reach the knockout rounds. That means a single defeat does not necessarily end your tournament. And it means that third-place finish, historically the most heartbreaking place in football, suddenly has genuine value.

## Who Gets In That Was Not Getting In Before

Africa goes from five spots to nine. Asia from four-and-a-half to eight-and-a-half. CONCACAF jumps from three-and-a-half to six. These are not just numbers. They are Mali, Uzbekistan, Jamaica. Countries with millions of football-obsessed people who have watched every World Cup on television and wondered when it would be their turn.

The counterargument that quality gets diluted misses the point. Nobody called the 1998 expansion from 24 to 32 teams a disaster. Croatia made the semi-finals in their debut. Senegal reached the quarter-finals in 2002. The smaller nations keep refusing to read the script they have been handed.

## The Path to the Trophy Gets Longer

To win in 2026, a team needs to win eight matches, not seven. That extra knockout game is a whole additional match under pressure, against a team who has earned their place and has nothing to lose.

For the giants, that is one more trap door. For everyone else, it is one more night they will never forget.

## What This Actually Felt Like

The 2026 World Cup final was played at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on July 19. One hundred and four matches across sixteen host cities. One hundred and four stories. And somewhere in there, a team nobody picked did something that made the world stop scrolling and watch.

More teams meant more of those moments. That was not a compromise. That was the whole point.

Alonso's Chelsea: 3-2, 4-3, then 2-1 at the Emirates
Seven goals in two wins, then a first loss. The start is loud. The defence is the argument.
Chelsea beat Fulham 3-2 and Brighton 4-3, then lost 2-1 at Arsenal. Rogers scored after 77 seconds in all three? No: inside five minutes in each of the first three.

## Why this start matters

Xabi Alonso's first three Premier League games scored like a pinball table. Fulham 2-3 Chelsea on 24 August. Chelsea 4-3 Brighton on 30 August. Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea on 6 September. Six points from nine. Eight goals scored, seven conceded. That is a personality, not a plan you put on a slide.

## What actually happened

Against Fulham, Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer scored in Alonso's first league match. Against Brighton, Romeo Lavia 4', Pedro Neto 14', Joao Pedro 32', Cole Palmer 74'. Brighton: Malick Yalcouye 35', a Joao Pedro own goal 63', Pascal Gross 90+6'. ESPN noted Brighton were the first side in 50 years to score three or more in four successive league games against Chelsea. They still lost.

At the Emirates, Rogers volleyed Chelsea ahead after 77 seconds. PremierLeague.com says Chelsea became the first team in Premier League history to score inside the opening five minutes in each of their first three games. Havertz equalised in the 25th. Odegaard won it after the break. Raya saved Estevao late. Alonso used the word suffering.

## What it changes

Chelsea are fourth on six points. Arsenal and City have nine. The attack is not the question. The question is whether a team that concedes seven in three can live in a title sentence. Matchweek 4 is Chelsea vs Hull. Hull have not conceded. That is the next test, not a result.
